Prompted the button provided in vmware doesn't work, can I download it from the cmd line
Oct 7, 2025, 9:18:10 AM EST

Yes, you can download and install VMware Tools from the command line inside your Windows VM if the menu button isn't working. This usually involves using a command-line tool like PowerShell to download the installer directly from VMware's public repository.

Here are two reliable methods to get it installed manually.

## Method 1: Download from the Command Line (PowerShell)

This is the most direct way to answer your question. You can use PowerShell within your Windows VM to download the installer and then run it.

  1. Open PowerShell as Administrator:

    • Click the Start Menu, type PowerShell, right-click "Windows PowerShell," and select "Run as administrator."

  2. Download the Installer:

    • First, find the latest version by visiting VMware's package repository in a browser: https://packages.vmware.com/tools/releases/
    • Click into the latest version folder (e.g., 12.4.0) and then into the windows folder. Find the link for the x64 or x86 .exe file.
    • Copy the link to the installer executable.
    • In your PowerShell window, use the Invoke-WebRequest command to download it. Paste the copied link in place of the example URL below.
    # This command downloads the installer to your current folder
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://packages.vmware.com/tools/releases/latest/windows/x64/VMware-tools-12.4.0-23259341-x86_64.exe" -OutFile "VMware-Tools-Installer.exe"

  3. Run the Installer:

    • Once the download is complete, you can run the installer directly from the same PowerShell window.
    # This command starts the installer you just downloaded
.\VMware-Tools-Installer.exe

  4. Complete Setup:

    • Follow the on-screen instructions in the installation wizard and reboot the VM when prompted.

## Method 2: Manually Mount the ISO from the Host

The "Install VMware Tools" button is just a shortcut to mount an ISO file that is already stored on your host computer. You can do this manually.

  1. Find the ISO on Your Host Machine:

    • On the computer running VMware Workstation/Fusion (your physical machine, not the VM), navigate to the VMware installation directory. The default location is usually:
    • C:\Program Files (x86)\VMware\VMware Workstation\
    • Inside this folder, you will find an ISO file named windows.iso. This is the disc image for the tools.

  2. Manually Mount the ISO:

    • In your VMware software, go to the settings for your Windows VM.
    • Select the CD/DVD Drive hardware.
    • Change the connection type to "Use ISO image file".
    • Click "Browse" and navigate to the windows.iso file you located in step 1.
    • Ensure the "Connected" checkbox is ticked.

  3. Install Inside the VM:

    • Go back to your running Windows VM.
    • Open File Explorer. The CD/DVD drive (usually D:) should now contain the VMware Tools installer.
    • Run setup64.exe to begin the installation and reboot when finished.

Prompted how to download vmware tools in windows box vmware
Oct 7, 2025, 9:17:23 AM EST

You don't typically need to download VMware Tools separately, as the installation files are already included with your VMware software (like Workstation, Fusion, or ESXi). The process involves "mounting" a virtual disc and running the installer from within your Windows virtual machine.

Here’s how to install it:

## 1. Mount the VMware Tools Virtual Disc

With your Windows virtual machine powered on and running, find the menu option to install VMware Tools. This varies slightly depending on your VMware product:

  • VMware Workstation: Go to VM > Install VMware Tools...
  • VMware Fusion: Go to Virtual Machine > Install VMware Tools
  • VMware vSphere/ESXi: Right-click the virtual machine and select Guest OS > Install VMware Tools...

This action connects a virtual CD/DVD to your VM that contains the necessary installation files.

## 2. Run the Installation Wizard

Once the virtual disc is mounted, the installer should start automatically inside your Windows VM.

  • If the installer begins, follow the on-screen prompts.
  • Choose the "Typical" setup type unless you have a specific reason to customize the installation.
  • Click "Install" to begin the process.

## 3. Manually Start the Installer (If Needed)

If the installer doesn't start on its own (which can happen if autorun is disabled), you'll need to start it manually:

  1. Inside your Windows VM, open File Explorer.
  2. Navigate to "This PC" or "Computer".
  3. You should see a new CD/DVD drive labeled "VMware Tools." Double-click it to start the installation.
  4. If double-clicking doesn't work, right-click the drive, select "Open," and then run the setup64.exe file (for 64-bit Windows) or setup.exe.

## 4. Reboot Your Virtual Machine

After the installation is finished, you will be prompted to restart your virtual machine. Click "Yes" to reboot. Once it restarts, VMware Tools will be active, and you should notice improved performance, better screen resolution, and features like drag-and-drop and copy-paste between your host and the VM.

Prompted I can ping my gateway with my linux box, i can ping my linux box with my windows box, but i can't ping my windows box with my linux on vmware
Oct 7, 2025, 9:12:24 AM EST

This is a classic networking puzzle, and the culprit is almost always the Windows Firewall on your host machine.

Your successful pings tell us a lot:

  • Linux VM to Gateway: Your VM has a proper IP address and can see the outside network.
  • Windows Host to Linux VM: Your VM's networking is configured correctly (likely Bridged or NAT), and the VM's internal firewall (if any) is allowing the ping.

The failure from the Linux VM to the Windows host points directly to the Windows machine refusing to answer the ping request.

## 🧱 The Most Likely Cause: Windows Firewall

By default, the Windows Firewall often blocks incoming ICMP Echo Requests (the technical term for pings), especially if your network profile is set to "Public."

How to Fix It

You need to enable a specific inbound rule to allow pings.

  1. On your Windows host, press the Windows Key and type wf.msc, then press Enter. This opens "Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security."
  2. In the left pane, click on Inbound Rules.
  3. Scroll down the list of rules and find File and Printer Sharing (Echo Request - ICMPv4-In).
    • You may see multiple rules for different profiles (Private, Public, Domain). You should enable the one for your active network profile (usually "Private"). To be certain, you can enable it for all profiles.
  4. Right-click the rule and select Enable Rule. The green checkmark icon should appear next to it.

Once enabled, try pinging your Windows host from the Linux VM again. It should now work.

## 🌐 Check Your VM's Network Configuration

If the firewall fix doesn't work, double-check how your VM's network adapter is configured in VMware.

  • Bridged: This is the most straightforward setting. The VM gets its own IP address on your local network, just like a separate physical computer. Your Windows host and Linux VM will be on the same subnet (e.g., 192.168.1.10 and 192.168.1.11). This is the recommended setting for what you're trying to do.
  • NAT (Network Address Translation): The VM is on a separate, private virtual network (e.g., 192.168.80.x), and VMware acts as a router to the main network. While your VM can ping out, pinging in to the host from the VM can sometimes be tricky because the request is coming from a different subnet, which the firewall is more likely to block.

You can check and change this in your VM's settings under the "Network Adapter" section.

## Troubleshooting Checklist

If you're still having issues, run through this quick list:

  1. Temporarily Disable Firewall: As a test, briefly disable the Windows Firewall for your network profile (Private or Public) and try to ping. Remember to re-enable it immediately after testing. If the ping works, you know 100% it's a firewall rule issue.
  2. Verify IPs: On your Windows host, open Command Prompt and type ipconfig. On your Linux VM, open a terminal and type ip addr show. Make sure you are pinging the correct IP address for the Windows machine's main network adapter (e.g., "Ethernet adapter" or "Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi").
  3. Switch to Bridged Mode: If you are using NAT, switch the VM's network adapter to Bridged, restart the VM's networking service or reboot the VM, and try again.
